June 15, 2026  
  
Dr. Mehmet Oz 
Administrator 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
Department of Health and Human Services 
7500 Security Boulevard 
Baltimore, MD 21244 
Submitted electronically via regulations.gov 
RE: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Interoperability 
Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Man-
aged Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and 
CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Ex-
changes [CMS-0062-P] 
 
Dear Administrator Oz, 
 
The Headache & Migraine Policy Forum (HMPF), a national coalition of more than two dozen 
stakeholder organizations in the migraine and headache disorder community, appreciates the 
opportunity to comment on the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ (CMS) proposed rule on 
interoperability standards and prior authorization for drugs, as well as the accompanying Request for 
Information on step therapy. HMPF shares CMS’ goal of modernizing utilization management so that 
tools such as prior authorization and step therapy no longer stand between patients and the treatments 
their clinicians have determined they need. 
Migraine is not only one of the most common neurological conditions affecting more than 40 million 
Americans, but it is also the second leading cause of disability globally.1 Despite its significant burden, 
migraine is frequently underdiagnosed, undertreated, and mischaracterized as a lifestyle issue rather 
than a serious neurological disease. Headache disorders and migraine diseases exist along a clinical 
spectrum, and treatment options and approaches are tailored based on the patient and the severity of 
the condition. Individual patients respond differently to available Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide 
(CGRP) therapies, and what works for one patient may be ineffective or poorly tolerated for another.  
 
For the millions of Americans living with migraine disease, excessive delays in treatment for migraine 
patients worsen patient outcomes and lead to higher costs to the health care system writ large.2 
Patients without access to effective treatment are more likely to experience emergency room visits, 
additional specialist appointments, and unnecessary medication trials.3 In fact, migraine patients are 
among the leading users of emergency department services; forcing patients to utilize emergency room 
 
1 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7708887/ 
2 https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/prior-authorization/prior-authorization-delays-care-and-in-
creases-health-care 
3 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25487421/ 
 
 
care to adequately treat their disease leads to downstream health and economic burdens for both the 
patient and for the overall health care system.4 
 
Chronic migraine is a neurological condition defined by the occurrence of 15 or more headache days 
each month over a period of at least three months, of which a minimum of 8 days per month satisfy the 
diagnostic criteria for migraine.5 Approximately 4 million Americans are estimated to live with chronic 
migraine.6 The condition disproportionately burdens women, who experience it at a rate roughly two to 
three times greater than men.7   
Prior authorization and step therapy are among the leading drivers of harmful delays for people im-
pacted by headache and migraine. When access to preventive therapy is held up by paperwork, patients 
can experience additional attacks, deteriorating mental health, missed work and school, and an inability 
to care for loved ones. These consequences are compounded by a workforce shortage in which patients 
often wait months for a neurology appointment,8 making it even more critical that once a clinical deci-
sion is finally reached, coverage processes do not impose additional delays in accessing treatment. 
Electronic Prior Authorization for Covered Treatments 
Several of the most important therapies in headache medicine, including botulinum toxin injections and 
infused CGRP-targeting agents, are often administered in the clinical setting and billed under the medi-
cal benefit. Authorization for these drugs still runs largely on phone calls, fax machines, and paper 
forms, followed by peer-to-peer appeals that pull clinicians away from patient care. HMPF therefore 
welcomes CMS’s proposal to extend electronic prior authorization requirements, expedite approval de-
cision timeframes, and require public reporting of prior authorization metrics. We view these provisions 
as crucial progress toward transparency and accountability for headache and migraine patients around 
the country.  
However, it is important to recognize that digitizing a flawed process is not the same as truly fixing it. A 
faster “no” does not help the patients living with these conditions. The measure of success must be 
whether Medicare beneficiaries actually receive their prescribed treatments more quickly and can track 
where their prior authorization or appeal requests are in the approval process. 
The administrative gauntlet itself can also distort prescribing practices. When clinicians anticipate that 
the most appropriate drug will likely trigger rounds of appeals and paperwork, many will steer toward 
whatever is most likely to be approved instead. In a 2025 American Medical Association survey, 95% of 
physicians said prior authorization delays care, 79% said it can lead patients to abandon treatment, and 
26% reported that it contributed to a serious adverse event for a patient in their care.9 
As CMS finalizes the rule, HMPF encourages CMS to: 
• 
Guarantee expedited review pathways for treatments when potential interruption risks rapid 
clinical deterioration, as is common in chronic migraine and cluster headache. 
 
4 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11426362/ 
5 https://ichd-3.org/1-migraine/1-3-chronic-migraine/  
6https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38700185/#:~:text=CM%20preva-
lence%20is%200.91%25%20(1.3,%2C%20and%2042.4%25%20in%202018.  
7 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38700185/ 
8 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39804477/ 
9 https://www.ama-assn.org/system/files/prior-authorization-survey.pdf 
 
 
• 
Prevent plans from circumventing decision timeframes through repeated requests for duplica-
tive documentation, ambiguous review “pauses,” or unclear rules about when the response 
timeline starts and stops. 
• 
Require that approvals remain valid for a clinically reasonable duration, absent a material 
change, and prohibit new authorization demands triggered solely by an adjustment in the dose 
or frequency of an already-approved therapy. 
• 
Ensure the framework accommodates clinically appropriate off-label prescribing, which remains 
common in headache medicine, and coordinates smoothly between pharmacy and medical ben-
efit systems. 
Prioritizing Continuity of Care  
Few experiences are more devastating for a patient than losing access to a therapy that is finally work-
ing, yet for many in the headache community, this happens routinely, whether through a formulary 
change, a new step therapy requirement, a prior authorization requirement, or a simple change of insur-
ance plan. Stability in chronic migraine and cluster headache is often hard-won after years of trial and 
error, and it can collapse quickly when treatment is interrupted. Patients should not be forced to relive a 
failed treatment history every time they change jobs, move, age into Medicare, have a different quali-
fied life event, or switch plans during open enrollment. 
HMPF urges CMS to embed continuity of care protections in the Final Rule, including specific protections 
for patients already stable on therapy, continuation of coverage while appeals are pending, and recogni-
tion of prior approvals when a patient transitions between health plans. 
Accessible and Transparent Reporting Requirements 
Prior authorization status data should be updated in as close to real time as possible and written in plain 
language patients can understand. Reporting metrics should be specific enough to convey exactly why a 
request was denied. For someone living with headache and migraine, weeks of uncertainty about 
whether treatment will be covered is itself a source of harm. 
Transparency must also extend upstream. Today, clinicians too often learn of a formulary change, a new 
step edit, or a point-of-care restriction only when a patient is turned away or a claim is denied. The Final 
Rule should require plans to give affected in-network clinicians timely electronic notice of utilization 
management and formulary changes. Public reporting, meanwhile, should be designed with patients in 
mind: approval and denial rates, appeal overturn rates, decision timelines, rates of repeat authorization 
for previously approved therapies, and step therapy requirement rates. These metrics should ideally be 
broken down by therapeutic category where possible, so beneficiaries can compare plans on whether 
needed care actually gets approved. 
Request for Information: Step Therapy 
Step therapy, the insurer practice commonly described as “fail first”, conditions coverage of a clinician’s 
chosen treatment on the patient first trying and failing one or more alternatives preferred by the health 
plan. In a recent survey published in the American Journal of Managed Care including over 500 physi-
cians, 79% of clinicians identified step therapy as a significant barrier to care.10 These protocols also rou-
 
10 https://doi.org/10.37765/ajmc.2024.89626 
 
 
tinely lag behind the clinical evidence: the American Headache Society’s 2024 position statement en-
dorses CGRP-targeting therapies as first-line preventive options without requiring failure on older drug 
classes, yet plans continue to demand exactly those failures.11 
HMPF urges CMS to treat step therapy as a core component of utilization management reform and to 
use this rulemaking to establish stronger guardrails: 
• 
Require plans to honor documented treatment failures and prior step therapy determinations, 
including those that occurred under a previous health plan, ensuring that no patient is ever 
made to fail twice on the same drug. 
• 
Mandate timely and accessible exceptions processes that defer to the treating clinician’s judg-
ment, with dedicated expedited pathways for urgent cases. 
• 
Set reasonable limits on the number of steps a plan may impose before covering the prescribed 
therapy. 
• 
Require plain language public disclosure of step therapy protocols during open enrollment. 
• 
Require step therapy protocols to be publicly available, regularly updated to reflect current spe-
cialty society guidelines, and applied through individualized review by clinicians with appropri-
ate expertise in neurological disease rather than one-size-fits-all algorithms. 
 
Conclusion 
The recommendations outlined above reflect both the evolving clinical evidence base and the lived ex-
periences of the millions of Americans managing headache and migraine. HMPF and its member organi-
zations are committed to ensuring that coverage policies keep pace with best practices, reduce unneces-
sary burdens on patients and clinicians alike, and support access to treatments that are proven to im-
prove quality of life. 
The stakes of this rulemaking are significant. For countless patients, prior authorization and step therapy 
continue to be two of the biggest obstacles in accessing care, and CMS now has an opportunity to ad-
dress them. We applaud CMS for this proposal, and ask that the Final Rule be built with patients at the 
center. We welcome feedback and extend an invitation for continued dialogue. Please do not hesitate to 
reach out with any questions at ksantiago@headachemigraineforum.org. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
Alliance for Patient Access 
American Migraine Foundation 
The Association of Migraine Disorders 
Chronic Migraine Awareness 
The Headache and Migraine Policy Forum 
National Headache Foundation 
U.S. Pain Foundation

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Headache & Migraine Policy Forum (HMPF), with signatories including Alliance for Patient Access, American Migraine Foundation, Association of Migraine Disorders, Chronic Migraine Awareness, National Headache Foundation, and U.S. Pain Foundation.
- **Stakeholder type:** Advocacy Group / Coalition.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** National coalition of more than two dozen stakeholder organizations in the migraine and headache disorder community; cites clinical literature, headache society guidance, and AMA survey data.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

HMPF supports CMS's effort to modernize prior authorization for drugs, especially for medical-benefit headache and migraine therapies such as botulinum toxin injections and infused CGRP-targeting agents. The commenter urges CMS to ensure electronic prior authorization reduces actual treatment delays rather than merely digitizing denials, and recommends stronger continuity-of-care, transparency, expedited review, and step therapy protections.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-USAGE-METRICS; TRANSPARENCY-related portions of API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING/API metrics; GENERAL RFI on step therapy.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** No CFR citations cited directly.
- **Standards referenced:** Electronic prior authorization generally; no specific FHIR IGs or NCPDP standards named.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Extend electronic prior authorization to covered migraine treatments**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support with modifications.
- **Rationale:** Many important headache therapies are administered in clinical settings and billed under the medical benefit; current authorization workflows rely on calls, faxes, forms, and peer-to-peer appeals that delay care and consume clinician time.
- **Specific request:** Finalize ePA expansion, but judge success by whether patients receive prescribed treatments faster and can track request/appeal status.

**Topic 2: Expedited and enforceable review pathways**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Modify / strengthen.
- **Rationale:** Interruptions in chronic migraine and cluster headache therapy can cause rapid clinical deterioration. Plans may circumvent deadlines through duplicative documentation requests or ambiguous review pauses.
- **Specific request:** Guarantee expedited pathways; define when timelines start and stop; prohibit repeated duplicative documentation and unclear pauses.

**Topic 3: Continuity of care and prior approvals**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify.
- **Rationale:** Patients stable on therapy can lose access because of formulary changes, new prior authorization or step therapy requirements, insurance changes, or plan transitions.
- **Specific request:** Protect stable patients, continue coverage while appeals are pending, recognize prior approvals during transitions, and prevent new authorization solely due to dose/frequency adjustments to already-approved therapy.

**Topic 4: Transparent reporting and patient-facing status information**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; TRANSPARENCY
- **Position:** Modify / clarify.
- **Rationale:** Patients and clinicians need plain-language, near-real-time status information and denial reasons; plan-comparison data should help beneficiaries understand whether needed care is approved.
- **Specific request:** Publicly report approval/denial rates, appeal overturn rates, timelines, repeat authorization rates, and step therapy rates, ideally by therapeutic category.

**Topic 5: Step therapy guardrails**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFI on step therapy
- **Position:** Modify / strengthen.
- **Rationale:** Step therapy can conflict with current clinical evidence, including American Headache Society recognition of CGRP-targeting therapies as first-line preventive options, and forces patients to repeat failures.
- **Specific request:** Honor documented failures and prior determinations across plans; provide timely exceptions; limit number of steps; disclose protocols in plain language; update protocols to specialty guidelines; use reviewers with neurologic expertise.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S12:** Addresses technical and workflow challenges for medical-benefit drugs, noting continued reliance on faxes, phone calls, forms, and peer-to-peer appeals for clinic-administered migraine therapies.
- **S15:** Addresses medical/pharmacy coordination by asking CMS to accommodate off-label prescribing and coordinate smoothly between pharmacy and medical benefit systems.
- **S16:** Responds to denial-reason transparency by asking that denial metrics and status data convey exactly why requests are denied in patient-understandable language.
- **S20/S43:** Supports expedited decision pathways and urges CMS to prevent plans from evading timelines through documentation games or ambiguous pauses.
- **S29/S35:** Recommends public reporting metrics that are patient-meaningful, including approval/denial rates, appeal overturn rates, decision timelines, repeat authorization rates, and step therapy rates.
- **S66-S82:** Responds to the step therapy RFI with detailed recommendations to honor prior failures and determinations, limit steps, update protocols to evidence, and require accessible exceptions.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize ePA requirements for drug therapies, especially those under the medical benefit.
2. Measure success by actual patient access and request/appeal tracking, not by faster denials alone.
3. Guarantee expedited review when treatment interruption risks rapid deterioration.
4. Prevent timeline evasion through repetitive documentation demands or ambiguous pauses.
5. Keep approvals valid for clinically reasonable periods and avoid new authorization for dose/frequency adjustments absent material change.
6. Accommodate clinically appropriate off-label prescribing.
7. Embed continuity-of-care protections, including coverage during appeals and recognition of prior approvals.
8. Require real-time or near-real-time, plain-language status and denial information.
9. Publicly report plan metrics meaningful to patients and clinicians, preferably by therapeutic category.
10. Establish step therapy guardrails that honor prior failures and align with specialty guidelines.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Digitizing flawed processes; delays to migraine and cluster headache therapy; unstable continuity of care; step therapy inconsistent with clinical evidence.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Additional migraine attacks, deteriorating mental health, missed work or school, inability to care for loved ones, emergency department use, and higher downstream costs.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Manual workflows, benefit-system coordination, payer documentation practices, lack of transparent status information, and lagging plan protocols.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** Migraine affects more than 40 million Americans and is the second leading cause of disability globally; approximately 4 million Americans live with chronic migraine; women experience chronic migraine at roughly two to three times the rate of men; AMA survey data cited 95% of physicians reporting PA delays care, 79% reporting treatment abandonment, and 26% reporting serious adverse events.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Literature on migraine disability, ED utilization, chronic migraine prevalence, neurologist access, AMA prior authorization survey, AJMC step therapy survey, and American Headache Society CGRP-targeting therapy position.
- **Examples provided:** Botulinum toxin injections and infused CGRP-targeting agents; plan transitions forcing patients to relive failed treatment history.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Migraine and headache patients, neurologists, headache specialists, clinicians, payers, pharmacies/PBMs, and plan enrollees.
- **Economic implications:** Delayed access may increase ED visits, specialist appointments, unnecessary medication trials, and broader system costs.
- **Technical feasibility:** Supports ePA but emphasizes operational details such as status tracking, benefit coordination, and documentation rules.
- **Patient care impact:** High; treatment delays and interruptions can worsen disease, function, mental health, and quality of life.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with strong modifications.
- **Tone:** Professional, patient-centered, evidence-based, and urgent.
- **Priority level:** High.

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "A faster 'no' does not help the patients living with these conditions." - Context: Warning that electronic prior authorization must improve outcomes, not just denial speed.
2. "Patients should not be forced to relive a failed treatment history every time they change jobs, move, age into Medicare, have a different qualified life event, or switch plans during open enrollment." - Context: Continuity-of-care argument.
3. "Prior authorization status data should be updated in as close to real time as possible and written in plain language patients can understand." - Context: Transparency recommendation.
4. "No patient is ever made to fail twice on the same drug." - Context: Step therapy guardrail recommendation.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Calls for enforceable expedited pathways and clear timeline rules.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Describes phone, fax, paperwork, and peer-to-peer appeals pulling clinicians from care.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Notes migraine burden among women and patient-centered access concerns, though equity is not the central frame.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Supports ePA but stresses real-world operational tracking and benefit coordination.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Central theme; delays and interruptions directly harm migraine patients.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Requests coordination between pharmacy and medical benefit systems.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Explicitly discusses therapies billed under medical benefit and coordination with pharmacy benefit.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Seeks plain-language status, denial reasons, public metrics, and formulary/UM change notices.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Critiques manual workflows and paperwork-driven processes.
